prompt:
Write one poem. Subject: forgetting. Form: a villanelle; the refrains may shift slightly each time they return if that serves the poem.

Before writing, settle privately on particulars: one place that could be found on a map, one object, one hour of the day. Build the poem out of things that can be seen, handled or overheard, and let any idea arrive through them. Do not name the emotion. Prefer the exact noun and the plain verb to the adjective. Leave out the furniture of generic verse: no tapestries, whispers, echoes, dances of light, souls or journeys; no moral; no closing epiphany. Break lines where the breath or the sense turns, not at every phrase. At least once, say something the previous line gave the reader no way to expect. End on an image, not a statement.

Output only the poem: no title, no commentary.
raw:
She asks again what time the ferry goes.
Four, I tell her. Four. She hunts the chain
of glasses hanging at her chest. It snows

on Stonington, on lobster traps in rows
along the pier, the co-op's yellow crane.
She asks me what time the ferry goes

and who I am to stand there in her clothes.
The coat is mine. Salt trucks grind up Main.
The glasses swing against her chest. It snows

into the dog's dish by the step. Nobody knows
to bring it in. We dug that grave in rain
ten Aprils back. What time the ferry goes

is taped beside the phone. She reads it, slows,
reads it aloud, then reads it once again,
her glasses, found, low on her nose. It snows.

The horn. She lifts her purse, sets it down, stows
one mitten in the breadbox. At the pane
she asks the glass what time the ferry goes.
The tape curls. Wharf lights come on. It snows.
